topic: The Geography of the Industrial Revolution
question: Why did the Industrial Revolution happen in Britain and not somewhere else?

cards.title: The British Origin
cards.question: Why did the transition to machine-powered production happen in Britain first?
cards.principle: Most people believe Britain industrialised first because of superior scientific genius or unique cultural institutions.
discarded: The assumption that British scientific or cultural superiority was the primary driver of mechanization.
cards.explanation: While Britain had inventors, France and China had equivalent or superior scientific communities. Ideas alone do not change global production; there must be a compelling economic reason to build expensive machines to do what hands already do.

cards.title: The Math of Machines
cards.question: Under what conditions does a business owner replace human workers with machines?
cards.principle: Mechanization is only profitable when the cost of fuel and capital is lower than the cost of the labor it replaces.
chain: Mechanization requires high wages relative to energy
cards.explanation: Early machines were highly inefficient, expensive to build, and broke down often. If labor is cheap, it is always more profitable to hire more people than to build a temperamental machine.

cards.title: The British Price Anomaly
cards.question: How did Britain's labor and energy prices compare to the rest of the world?
cards.principle: Eighteenth-century Britain had the highest wages in the world alongside the cheapest energy on earth.
chain: Mechanization requires high wages relative to energy
Britain had uniquely high wages and cheap coal
cards.explanation: In London, wages were twice as high as in Paris or Florence, and many times higher than in Beijing. Meanwhile, British coal was vastly cheaper than wood or coal anywhere else in Europe or Asia.
cards.takeaway: Britain was uniquely incentivized to substitute coal for people.

cards.title: The Origin of High Wages
cards.question: Why were British wages so high and its energy so cheap?
cards.principle: Global trade empires drove up British wages, while geology made British coal uniquely accessible.
chain: Mechanization requires high wages relative to energy
Britain had uniquely high wages and cheap coal
Trade raised wages while geology kept coal cheap
cards.explanation: Britain's success in international trade created a massive boom in London, driving up wages across the country. To heat these growing cities, Britain turned to coal, which was cheap because massive deposits lay right next to the sea and navigable rivers.
cards.takeaway: Geography and empire created the price gap.

cards.title: The Pithead Economy
cards.question: What was the physical bottleneck that prevented other coal-rich regions from industrializing?
cards.principle: Early steam engines were so inefficient they could only be run where fuel was essentially free: at the mouth of a coal mine.
chain: Mechanization requires high wages relative to energy
Britain had uniquely high wages and cheap coal
Trade raised wages while geology kept coal cheap
Early engines required zero-cost fuel at the mine
cards.explanation: The first steam engines converted less than one percent of coal's energy into work. They were used to pump water out of flooded coal mines. Because they sat on top of the coal mine, the fuel they burned was waste coal that cost nothing to transport. No other industry could afford to run them.
cards.takeaway: The steam engine was born at the only place it was economically viable.

cards.title: The Efficiency Cycle
cards.question: How did a crude mine-pump turn into a global industrial revolution?
cards.principle: Operating inefficient engines at coal mines allowed engineers to gradually improve their efficiency until they were cheap enough to run elsewhere.
chain: Mechanization requires high wages relative to energy
Britain had uniquely high wages and cheap coal
cards.explanation: Because Britain had a massive coal mining industry, it could afford to run thousands of highly inefficient early engines. This massive user base provided the cash and the practical testing ground for inventors to make engines efficient enough to power textile mills far away from the mines.

cards.title: The Necessity of Inefficiency
cards.question: What does this tell us about how major technological transitions occur?
cards.principle: Breakthrough technologies are almost always too inefficient for general use; they require a highly specific, local economic subsidy to survive their infancy.
cards.explanation: If Britain did not have flooded coal mines right next to cheap coal, the steam engine would have been a useless invention. It survived and evolved only because there was one specific place on earth where extreme inefficiency did not matter. History is shaped by the physical spaces that tolerate crude first drafts.
cards.takeaway: Innovation needs a localized economic subsidy.

followups: Why did China, which had massive coal deposits and advanced technology, not develop the steam engine first?
How did the transition to coal-powered shipping change the balance of global trade wages?
What is the modern equivalent of the coal mine pithead where highly inefficient new technologies are currently being subsidized by local conditions?
